title: Palsgraf v. Long Island Railroad Co.

history.title: Initial consultation
history.instruction: Interview the client or railroad representative and identify what must be investigated. Do not assume evidence not in the record.

history.title: Investigation
history.instruction: Examine the incident, distinguish observations from inference, and develop a viable negligence theory.

history.title: Theory & pleadings
history.instruction: State the client's claim or defense. Identify duty, breach, causation and injury, and the strongest counterargument.

history.title: Trial advocacy
history.instruction: Prepare a short oral submission and respond to questions from the trial judge; distinguish facts from speculation.

history.title: Court of Appeals
history.instruction: Make a concise appellate argument from the disclosed record. The eventual 1928 disposition remains sealed.

history.title: Historical reveal & review
history.instruction: Compare arguments to the actual decision. Discuss Cardozo's majority and Andrews's dissent, then consider a role reversal.

facts.text: The incident took place at the East New York station on August 24, 1924.
Helen Palsgraf was waiting on the platform as a passenger.
Railroad employees were assisting a passenger who was attempting to board a train.
A package carried by the boarding passenger fell from his possession.
The package contained fireworks that exploded after it fell.
The package's appearance did not give notice of its explosive contents.
The explosion caused scales on the platform to fall, injuring Palsgraf.
A jury verdict for Palsgraf awarded $6,000 in 1927.

reveal.disposition: The New York Court of Appeals reversed the judgment in favor of Palsgraf.
reveal.majority: Chief Judge Benjamin Cardozo's majority understood negligence as relational: the plaintiff's right depends on a foreseeable risk of harm to that plaintiff; on these facts, no duty was breached toward Palsgraf.
reveal.dissent: Judge William Andrews's dissent treated the negligent act as a wrong to the world at large and located the question of the extent of liability mainly in proximate cause.
